**Summary:** The table material in this paper is largely formal/architectural rather than empirical, yielding no quantitative benchmarks, method comparisons, or performance metrics. The extractable content supports four main findings. (1) Table 1 illustrates the GP 2 execution model, in which a graph program is executed via an `Execute` operation to transform an input host graph into an output graph. (2) Table 2 outlines the implementation toolchain — a GP 2-to-C compiler feeding GCC and a runtime system — linking program, graph, and executable representations. (3) Table 3 defines two primitive host-graph navigation operations, `firstHostNode(m)` and `nextHostNode(m)`, for enumerating nodes carrying a mark `m`. (4) Table 4 extends this to six primitives for marked edges (first/next in-edge, out-edge, and loop edge), and — the paper's only quantitative claim in tabular form — establishes that all eight node- and edge-navigation primitives run in guaranteed **O(1)** constant time, implying a mark-indexed adjacency structure supporting efficient mark-filtered graph traversal. Tables 5 and 6 were not recoverable as data (one extraction artifact, one mis-detected formal rule fragment), so no further experimental findings can be reported. In sum, the tables substantiate the asymptotic cost model of the paper's core graph-access API rather than any experimental evaluation.
